newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels and government come face-to-face on hostages.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels and government come face-to-face on hostages.

text.p: A member of the Marxist MRTA rebel group holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima and a Peruvian government negotiator are due to meet face-to-face on Tuesday in a bid to end Peru's tense 56-day siege.

Red Cross officials have raised their flag over a house opposite the residence where the number two of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) will meet President Alberto Fujimori's negotiator Education Minister Domingo Palermo.

Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a key mediator in the hostage crisis, told reporters on Monday: "I hope that once and for all we will find a way out of this situation, that has been affecting all of us for a long time now."
The head of Peru's Catholic Church, Bishop Augusto Vargas Alzamora, said he hoped the talks "will result in the liberation of all the hostages and a peaceful ending without the loss of lives."

MRTA chief Nestor Cerpa Cartolini on Monday voiced his "total willingness to start conversations" to end the long siege that begun on Dec. 17, when 15 heavily-armed MRTA rebels stormed the residence during a cocktail party and seized over 500 guests.

It later freed most of them but kept prized captives including two Peruvian government ministers, Fujimori's brother Pedro, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, top Peruvian security and court officials and Japanese businessmen.

Cerpa, who will be represented by his second-in-command Roli Rojas, known by the nom de guerre "El Arabe" (The Arab), made it clear however that he would not withdraw his "irrevocable" demand -- the release of 400 MRTA comrades from Peruvian jails.

As the Red Cross made preparations including laying cables between the two buildings and erecting tarpaulins to hide Rojas from view when he boards an armoured van for the talks, Cerpa made declarations by walkie-talkie from inside the residence.

He accused Fujimori, currently on a visit to London, of making a "veiled threat" to use force if the talks failed and said he was still as "determined to face a peaceful or military solution with the same conviction" as when he began the siege.
The threat of bloodshed, disguised by musical duels over loudspeakers between police and rebels in recent weeks, was made plain on Monday by an explosion followed by gunfire.

Police said an animal stepped on a landmine in the compound planted by the MRTA, prompting the rebels to open fire. But the MRTA said they had tossed out a grenade and fired shots to ward off police special forces and sharpshooters surrounding them.
"There was a burst of gunfire but we don't know the reason," said Interior Minister Juan Briones Davila. "The main thing is that the hostages are fine and weren't hurt."

Fujimori has called the planned meeting, which will be in the presence of mediators from the Church, Red Cross, Canada and a Japanese observer, "preliminary talks" to pave the way for "definitive talks, probably with Cerpa Cartolini himself."

The government and rebels have not met face-to-face since Palermo met Cerpa in the residence in late December. Fujimori's refusal to consider the release of MRTA guerrillas has stymied attempts at fresh talks. He also rules out paying a ransom, but has talked of possible asylum abroad for the hostage-takers.

Fujimori's tough stance, praised by U.S. President Bill Clinton and British Prime Minister John Major, also has support in Peru where guerrilla violence has cost about 25,000 lives in the past 16 years. A poll published on Monday showed 86 percent also oppose freeing MRTA prisoners to end the hostage crisis.

Cerpa made it clear on Monday that the peace process would not be easy: "The beginning of the talks does not necessarily mean the beginning of the solution to the conflict." His negotiator, Rojas, is a 34-year-old former transport worker who joined the MRTA while a university student. Jailed in 1986, he tunneled out to freedom in 1990 and became Cerpa's right-hand man.
